title: Decorator (structural)
points: Adds behaviour to an object by wrapping it in another object that implements the same interface.
The wrapper forwards calls to the wrapped object and adds its own logic before or after, with no change to the original class.
Main benefit: prevents subclass explosion. Features are combined at runtime instead of one subclass per combination.
trade: OCP: a new feature is a new wrapper. Inheritance needs up to 2^n classes for n optional features; decorators need n. Downsides: many small classes, wrapping order matters, harder to debug through layers. Strategy swaps how one thing is done; Decorator layers extra behaviour and can stack. Examples: BufferedReader(new FileReader(...)), Spring AOP proxies.
test: You have EmailNotifier and SmsNotifier, and want any combination of logging, retry and encryption. How many subclasses would inheritance need, and how does Decorator avoid that? Does wrapping order matter?
answer: Inheritance needs a subclass for every combination, up to 2^3 = 8 per base notifier. Decorator needs 3 wrappers that you stack at runtime. Yes, order matters: retry around logging logs once, logging around retry logs every attempt.

questions.question: You want any combination of logging, retry and encryption on top of EmailNotifier and SmsNotifier, without a subclass for every combination. Which pattern?
questions.explanation: Decorator: stackable wrappers implementing the same interface. It avoids subclass explosion by composing features at runtime.
